routes.speaker: Rowan Williams
routes.position: Christian theism: God is the transcendent source and context of reality

bridges.statement: God best accounts for reality as its transcendent creative source and the context within which finite explanation occurs, not as a competing item within the universe.
Consciousness and aesthetic meaning disclose depths and connections not exhausted by a reductive description of matter.
Creation is God's continuous sustaining act, compatible with a self-developing evolutionary world rather than an episodic intervention.
Classical divine simplicity denies composition, external conditioning, and derivation, so it is not equivalent to low functional complexity.
Christian resurrection hope answers suffering by opening solidarity and a future in which destructiveness is not final.
Belief in divine order can enlarge rather than cancel responsibility for scientific discovery.
Faith is formed and revised through accumulated lived encounters that resist reduction to a single formulaic test.

routes.speaker: Richard Dawkins
routes.position: Scientific naturalism: science and natural selection explain reality without God

bridges.statement: Science explains complex reality from primordial simplicity, with natural selection supplying the apparent engineering of life without God.
Consciousness is an evolved manifestation of brain physiology and provides no basis for postmortem survival.
The ruthless suffering intrinsic to natural selection counts against a beneficent divine designer and a human-centered incarnation.
Any intelligence capable of devising laws, constants, and providential acts must possess explanatory complexity and cannot be ultimately simple.
Human art and abstract thought are emergent overflow capacities of brains selected for survival and reproduction.
Introducing a designer undermines the scientific responsibility to explain complexity through models and theories.
God is an erroneous but scientific hypothesis whose truth would transform science rather than occupy a separate magisterium.
